slides.title: Clickjacking
slides.summary: An attacker loads your site in an invisible iframe and tricks the user into clicking your buttons.
body: Clickjacking (UI redressing) loads your page in a transparent iframe over a decoy button. The user thinks they're clicking “Claim prize”, but they click “Confirm transfer” on your site, while logged in.
<mark>If anyone can frame your site, any one-click action is at risk.</mark>
Tell the browser who may frame you:

ul: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none': nobody may frame this page.
X-Frame-Options: DENY: the legacy header. Send it too for old browsers; frame-ancestors wins where both are supported.

body.note: JavaScript “frame-busting” code is unreliable: the framing page can block it with a sandboxed iframe. Use the headers.

figure.alt: Three panels. Left, what the user sees: a page on evil.example offering a prize with a big Claim prize button. Middle, what is really there: the same decoy page, with your banking page loaded in an iframe set to opacity 0 exactly on top of it, so its Confirm transfer button sits over the Claim prize button; the click goes to your page, with the user's cookies. Right, with Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors none: the browser refuses to render your page in the frame, the iframe is empty and the click does nothing.

slides.title: Embedding other sites safely
slides.summary: When you frame someone else's content, sandbox it and give it only the permissions it needs.
body: The other direction matters too. Widgets, ads, previews and user-supplied embeds run code you don't control.

ul: sandbox with no value blocks scripts, forms, popups, top-level navigation and same-origin access. Add back only what's needed.
Never combine allow-scripts with allow-same-origin for content from your own origin: the frame can then remove its own sandbox.
allow grants powerful features (camera, payment, fullscreen) to that one frame.
referrerpolicy, loading="lazy" and a title limit leaks, save bandwidth and help screen readers.

body: <mark>Treat any iframe as untrusted: start from a full sandbox and add permissions one at a time.</mark>

body.more: Rendering user HTML in an iframe
body.text: For untrusted HTML such as email bodies, serve it from a separate, sandboxed origin (e.g. usercontent.example). Even if a script runs there, it can't touch your app's cookies or DOM.

cells.text: Navigating your page, only after a click

slides.title: Talking to iframes with postMessage
slides.summary: postMessage crosses origins safely only if both sides check who they're talking to.
body: window.postMessage is the safe way to talk across origins, but it's a common source of DOM XSS when origins aren't checked.

ul: Sending: pass an exact targetOrigin. Never use '*' for anything sensitive.
Receiving: check event.origin against an exact allowlist before reading event.data. Don't use includes() or endsWith().
Validate the data like any other input. Never pass it to innerHTML, eval or location.

body: <mark>A message listener with no origin check accepts data from every site that can open or frame your page.</mark>

figure.alt: A parent page at app.example.com embeds an iframe from widget.example. The parent calls postMessage with targetOrigin https://widget.example, so the browser only delivers the message if the frame really is that origin. The widget's message listener checks event.origin equals https://app.example.com before using the data. A third window at evil.example also posts a message to the widget; the widget's origin check rejects it. Using '*' as targetOrigin or skipping the origin check lets any site send or receive these messages.
